draft.title: What food security means
card: Food security means everyone can always get enough safe, healthy food. It is about people, not only about how much food a country grows.
enough food has to be grown or brought in. A poor harvest can shrink the supply.
people must be able to afford the food. Food on the shelves does not help a family that cannot pay for it.
food has to get to the people who need it. Damaged roads or a long distance from shops can stop it.
draft.remember: Food security needs enough food, the means to buy it and a way for it to arrive.

a.q: Which situation shows a problem with people being able to afford food?
opts: Shops are full, but many families cannot pay the prices
A flood cuts the only road to a remote town
A drought leaves farms with very small harvests
A town has no shop within a day's travel
a.why: Food is available in the shops, but families cannot buy it, so the problem is affordability. The flooded road is a problem of food reaching people, and the drought is a problem of supply.
a.clue: Think about food that is there but out of a family's budget.

b.q: Farms near Karratha, Western Australia, grow plenty of food, and local families can afford it. A cyclone then floods the roads for weeks, so trucks cannot deliver to a remote community. Which part of food security has failed there?
opts: Food is not reaching the people who need it
Too little food is being grown in the region
Families can no longer afford to buy food
The food on offer is no longer safe to eat
b.why: The food exists and people can pay for it, but the flooded roads stop it arriving. So the problem is that food is not reaching people. Low supply is the tempting answer, but the farms are still producing.
b.clue: The food exists and can be paid for. What has stopped?

a.best: Shops are full, but many families cannot pay the prices

b.best: Food is not reaching the people who need it

problems.detail: Karratha is in the arid Pilbara, where there is very little farming. 'Farms near Karratha grow plenty of food' is not realistic, so WA students may find it odd. Most food there is trucked in from Perth. A real farming area, or food trucked from Perth, would fit better.
The stem first says 'local families can afford it', then moves to 'a remote community'. It is unclear whether these are the same people. Both parts of the scenario should refer to the same community.

The card uses 'Access' only for affordability and makes getting food to people a separate 'Reach'. In the standard (FAO) definition, access covers both economic and physical access. Students may be confused when they meet 'access' in other sources.
